title: Spectral Energy Balancer
description: Two mystical artifacts—an animated interpolation totem and a scattering skull—are linked by a shared energy pool of 100 units. The user redistributes energy between them using sliders and color channels, where energy given to one must be taken from the other. Full undo/redo history tracks every adjustment, and the visual state of both models reflects the current energy distribution in real time.
prompt: Create a single HTML file using Three.js r170 (via importmap from cdn.jsdelivr.net) that loads InterpolationTest.glb on the left and ScatteringSkull.glb on the right, spaced 3 units apart. Use a PerspectiveCamera at (0,2,6) looking at origin, with OrbitControls. Add ambient light (0.4) and two directional lights. Implement a conservation-based energy system: a shared pool of exactly 100 energy units split across R, G, B channels (initially 33, 33, 34). Create an HTML overlay panel with 3 paired sliders per channel (R/G/B), each pair controlling how much of that channel goes to the left model vs right model. The constraint is: leftR + rightR = totalR for each channel, and totalR + totalG + totalB = 100 always. Add a master slider that redistributes total energy across channels while preserving the left/right ratios within each channel. Apply energy visually: the InterpolationTest model's emissive color intensity and animation timeScale scale with its total energy (sum of its RGB). The ScatteringSkull's material opacity (use transparent materials), emissive glow color, and scale (0.5 to 1.5) respond to its total energy. When one model gains energy it visually intensifies while the other dims. Implement full undo/redo: store snapshots of all 6 values (3 channels × 2 models) on every slider release. Bind Ctrl+Z for undo and Ctrl+Y for redo, with on-screen buttons too. Display current energy values numerically for both models. Play InterpolationTest animations via AnimationMixer. Add a 'Pulse Transfer' button that animates 10 energy units flowing from the higher-energy model to the lower one over 1 second with a visible particle arc between them. The total must remain 100 at all times—this is the conservation law. Show a warning if any rounding error breaks conservation.
